data.title: Trump weighs in on Flock debate: 'I like them'
data.description:
President Trump on Sunday backed the use of Flock cameras, a controversial surveillance tool.

“Speaking of [artificial intelligence], Flock cameras. You haven’t talked a lot about these Flock cameras. A lot of law enforcement say they really help them. Would you be willing to back that?” a reporter asked Trump on Air Force One.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president responded, adding later, “I like them.”

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems operated by Flock Safety has grown on both sides of the aisle.

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database. That database logs license plate numbers, as well as car features like make, model, color and bumper stickers. Local jurisdictions can share data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that law enforcement can use in crime solving.

Earlier this month, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been on the president’s bad side in the last few years, unveiled a bill aimed at limiting federal funds used for automated license plate reader cameras (ALPRs) and biometric surveillance cameras.

The legislation, named the Flock-Off Act, would halt any effort to buy, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities or local law enforcement.

“Federal taxpayers should not be forced to fund the surveillance state,” Massie said in a post on the social platform X, in which he discussed the bill.

data.title: Sydney Sweeney criticized by women athletes for nude sports prediction market ad
data.description:
Actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from a growing number of female athletes online over a new advertisement for a sports prediction market platform in which she appears wearing little or no clothing.

The advertisement, promoting prediction market platform NoVig, opens with a nude Sweeney asking the camera “think you know sports? Prove it,” while holding two footballs in front of her chest.

In another series of shots, Sweeney sits atop a basketball hoop, crouches in front of a hockey goal keeper’s net and lies on a soccer bench, all with limited or no clothing on.

Several female professional athletes, across a wide array of sports, are expressing outrage at the less than one-minute ad, arguing it objectifies women in sports and is in poor taste.

“idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing but this is what a women in sports looks like,” the American gymnast Gracie Kramer wrote in one post on Instagram, which she captioned “because it really is that deep.”

Skye Nicolson, an Australian professional boxer wrote Sweeney was “giving the ad campaign exactly what they wanted, but honestly these companies need to do better.”

Australian surfer Felicity Palmateer told CNN she found the ad to be “very damaging” for female athletes.

“Just absolute utter disbelief, incredibly disappointing, like, how far you can put women’s sports backwards in the space of a 42-second commercial,” Palmateer said.

Sweeney has not commented publicly on the backlash the ad is receiving, but she reportedly approached NoVig about participating in the ad and the company’s CEO told Front Office Sports she was “great at captivating audiences and being the center of attention.”

The actress has been at the center of controversy in the past, most recently in connection with an advertisement for American Eagle jeans which some critics said smacked of promoting eugenics.

Sweeney told Variety at the time of her work promoting various brands, “I’ve always believed that I’m not here to tell people what to think.”

data.title: Watch live: Jeffries gives remarks as AI safety concerns mount
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) will speak with reporters Monday afternoon as calls for guardrails around artificial intelligence (AI) build after industry experts raised red flags around safety of the emerging technology.

Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) have pressed the Trump administration for transparency on how the U.S. will respond to potential threats from AI and what potential regulations could look like. President Trump and GOP leaders have largely brushed off the fears.

His remarks also come as the House faces a shrinking legislative calendar ahead of the November midterms and as Democrats seek to take control of Congress next year.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' confined migrants in 'small metal enclosures': DHS internal watchdog
data.description:
A new report reviewing the conditions at the now-closed Alligator Alcatraz center in Florida slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to meet a variety of federal standards, describing “unprecedented” treatment of migrants, including containing them in cages about the size of a phone booth.

The Monday report from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) is the first such federal review of the facility, which is referred to in the report as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility.

The report describes alarming conditions, including unhygienic practices for food and water as well as limited opportunities for migrants to bathe themselves.

OIG said Alligator Alcatraz provided half the living space for migrants required under federal law – just 28 square feet when the facility was at max capacity, far from the 75-square-foot mandate.

ICE officials also used cages that were roughly 4 feet by 4 feet as “‘calming areas’ for detainees to deescalate and have time alone.”

“FSSF confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures — each offering about 18 square feet of floor space — for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly 2 hours, a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities. The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” OIG wrote.

OIG found that in at least one documented case, a migrant was put in the small cages as a punishment.

The report generated swift blowback from immigration advocates who targeted ICE’s explanation for the small cages.

“There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike,” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge, a refugee resettlement agency, said in a statement.

“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food, and basic hygiene — and in at least one case locked in a cage as punishment. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty, carried out in our name and on our dime, to the tune of more than a million dollars a day.” 

OIG said they were unable to “independently confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding their use of the enclosures” as well as other allegations, such as deprivation of food or water issues described in a prior Amnesty International report, as none of the detainees interviewed while OIG was there reported those conditions.

“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG. Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being,” the watchdog wrote.

Both ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to request for comment.

In the report, however, the agency and department placed much of the responsibility for the facility with Florida, despite it being constructed with federal funds and managed by ICE agents.

“While FEMA provided funding for the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF) under the Shelter and Services Program, DHS did not have a contract with Florida to manage the detention space within the facility. The State of Florida authorized the repurposing of the center from the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport into a state detention center,” DHS officials wrote in a letter in response to the report.

data.title: Lowering gas prices requires stopping climate shakedowns
data.description:
On Sept. 1, just as the national average for gasoline hit $4.09 a gallon, President Trump brought oil refiners and fuel distributors to the White House to discuss expanding refining capacity and bringing prices down. Administration officials said the conversation included “concrete ways to expand capacity, including regulation changes, faster permitting and additional investments.”

Removing federal barriers to new projects is a good place to start, as American refineries are already operating at nearly 97 percent of capacity. But permits alone will only go so far. Unless something is done to stop state governments and foreign regulators from sabotaging American energy dominance, the price at the pump, not to mention U.S. national security, will suffer. 

In blue states and municipalities here in the United States, an unholy alliance of progressive officials and their cabal of climate litigators have weaponized climate lawsuits and “Climate Superfunds” to bleed the industry of billions of dollars. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, European regulators are forcing costly climate mandates into American supply chains.

Together, these forces are inflicting an unnecessary burden on our energy industry at a time when U.S. energy dominance matters most. All of this raises costs that get passed on to consumers and makes new refinery investments harder to justify. Any serious effort to lower gas prices and expand refining capacity has to stop the lawsuits, retroactive charges, and foreign mandates driving rising costs.

To Trump’s credit, his executive order last year directed the Justice Department to identify and challenge ideologically motivated state laws burdening domestic energy production. His administration has since challenged New York’s and Vermont’s “Climate Superfund” laws as well as climate actions in Hawaii and Michigan. That pushback paid off last month when a federal judge blocked the New York superfund, which sought $75 billion in retroactive charges against oil and gas companies based on fossil fuels legally produced and sold between 2000 and 2018.

Vermont’s Climate Superfund, however, remains very much alive, and other states could easily pass their own versions.

Beyond the climate superfund laws, blue states and municipalities are also bleeding energy companies dry in court over damages tied to decades of global emissions. California alone sued five major oil companies and the American Petroleum Institute in 2023 for allegedly “deceiving the public about climate change,” while Multnomah County, Ore., is seeking nearly $52 billion from oil and gas companies over the 2021 heat wave. Hawaii filed one last year alleging “harm to public trust resources,” while Michigan filed this year, accusing the industry of a “conspiracy” to “restrict the development of renewable energy and electric vehicles.”

Whatever the theory, these lawsuits force a handful of American energy companies to spend millions defending themselves in local courts, while losing even a few could expose the industry to hundreds of billions in liability and allow local courts to set energy policy for the rest of the country.

Rather than leave energy companies and the Justice Department to keep fighting the same battle one state and one courtroom at a time, Trump can and should put his full weight behind Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Rep. Harriet Hageman’s (R-Wyo.) Stop Climate Shakedowns Act. The legislation would prohibit climate lawsuits in state and federal court and void state energy-penalty laws such as the climate superfunds.

But even then, the administration must still deal with our friends across the Atlantic, where the European Union is using its Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive to require American companies that operate there to police environmental practices throughout their entire supply chains under the threat of fines.

As Rep. Craig Goldman (R-Texas) has noted, a gas-station owner in Fort Worth could get pulled into Europe’s mandates simply because his franchise agreement is with an American fuel company that operates there. The owner does no business in Europe and has no representation there, and yet he could still get stuck paying the compliance costs Europe adds to his contract.

Fortunately, a solution is waiting in the wings here too. The PROTECT USA Act, now before Congress, would stop foreign governments from forcing their sustainability rules on American companies. Goldman’s Stop the EU Overreach Act would also direct the U.S. trade representative to investigate whether the EU directives unfairly restrict American businesses and determine how the United States should respond. Trump should do everything in his power to push both forward alongside the Stop Climate Shakedowns Act.

Pressing refiners to expand capacity should absolutely be part of Trump’s effort to lower gasoline prices. But faster permits and regulatory relief will not be enough to justify billion-dollar investments while blue states pursue retroactive climate charges and European regulators add new costs to American supply chains.

If the administration wants refiners to invest and consumers to pay less, it must stop hostile governments from piling new costs onto American energy companies.

Jason Isaac is the CEO of the American Energy Institute. He previously served four terms in the Texas House of Representatives.

data.title: Donald Trump Jr.'s wife defends wedding gift from Russian oligarch
data.description:
Influencer and model Bettina Trump, the wife of Donald Trump Jr., defended the couple’s wedding gift given to them by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev.

“Apparently our wedding is making headlines again, so a little clarity seems in order,” Bettina Trump wrote on Instagram. “Don and I got married privately … surrounded ONLY by our family. It was intimate, deeply personal and one of the most beautiful days of our lives.”

ProPublica first reported that the Caribbean-set wedding was heavily funded by Kremlev — who has ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin — was among the roughly 50 people at the private ceremony. The billionaire has been regarded as an adversary of the U.S., has been accused of attempting to influence American elections and was recently seen in China as part of a delegation with Putin.

Retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr. told the outlet that oligarchs typically work in coordination with the Russian government.

“If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something,” Montoya noted, adding that, “This should be unthinkable for the son of the president. End of story.”

Bettina Trump wrote that Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”

“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” she continued. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”

The new wife of President Trump’s eldest son shared photos of their wedding, quipping that she did this because “fake news travels fast.” Many of the photos shared by the Trumps do not include any of the Russian guests, though the top of Kremlev’s head can be seen in a photo shared by a friend of hers.

“So, for anyone determined not to let the facts get in the way of a good story: NO CONSPIRACY , NO MYSTERY,” Bettina wrote. “Just a private family wedding, a wonderful weekend with friends and one hell of a party.”

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. did not dispute Kremlev’s wedding payments to ProPublica and said he was a personal friend of the president’s son. He added that Kremlev is “not someone he has a business relationship with” and said they bonded over their interest in boxing and the outdoors.

Their engagement was first announced in December. The president was unable to attend the May wedding, telling reporters at the time that he felt it was important to stay in Washington.

“He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair, and I’m going to try and make it. I’m in the midst — I said, ‘You know, this is not good timing for me, I have a thing called Iran and other things,'” Trump said, referring to the Iran war.

data.title: Brothers rescue group of elderly people from burning California assisted living facility
data.description:
(KTLA) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday.

Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m.

As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from the home, neighbors Alex Bazinyan, 20, and his brother Narek Bazinyan, 15, realized time was of the essence and decided to run over and help.

“I ran outside and I was looking at the front door when I saw the nurse outside and she was screaming for help,” Alex told Nexstar’s KTLA’s John Fenoglio.

The brothers knew several people were trapped inside the home that was operating as an assisted living facility for seniors.

Narek initially grabbed a garden hose to help quell the flames, but as the blaze grew more intense and screams for help grew louder, they knew they had to run into the fire.

“I go inside this big room and I see all these old people on the floor with catheters,” Alex recalled. “Some people were injured, had blood on their legs. We just took everybody out one by one.”

There were eight people inside the home — two nurses and six elderly residents, most of whom were unable to walk. The brothers said the nurses were desperately trying to remove the elderly residents from the home but were struggling.

“I see a guy in the back about to be engulfed by the flames,” Narek recalled when he entered the home. “The nurse is trying to pick him up. I go and grab his legs and pull him out to the front.”

Soon after, two additional neighbors also ran over to help evacuate the residents.

“As I’m looking around, I just see flames going up and coming towards me,” Narek said. “I tried bringing everyone out as fast as I could. There was smoke everywhere. I was pretty much blinded by the smoke.”

The brothers were able to safely rescue all six elderly residents and placed them on the front lawn as they awaited fire crews.

But just as they moved the last person out of the burning home, Alex recalled hearing a loud explosion. 

“I heard an explosion come from the house,” he said. “I looked back and I didn’t understand what exploded, but I just heard a big boom.”

Firefighters arrived at the home and were able to extinguish the flames before any nearby houses were affected. The Glendale Fire Department chief said an oxygen tank likely exploded, which collapsed part of the home. 

Seven people were transported to the hospital with minor injuries. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

As for Alex and Narek, they said their instincts just kicked in and the only thing they were focused on was quickly rescuing everyone from the burning home.

“It’s that instinct of whenever you see people in need, you want to help them out,” Alex said. “You don’t really think about who it is. We have a really tight-knit community here.”

Narek agreed, saying, “If you ever see anyone in need, you should always try to help them out as much as you can.”

data.title: Kennedy Center could close as early as Tuesday as officials warn of impending 'fiscal collapse'
data.description:
The Kennedy Center board is set to vote Tuesday on whether to immediately close the institution’s main building for renovations, as a court battle over renewed attempts to add President Trump’s name to the facility persists.

Officials have warned that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks” if it is unable to publicly recognize Trump’s fundraising role, according to a copy of a draft resolution contained in court filings.

“The Board understand that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the resolution states.

The document describes the Kennedy Center as on the brink of bankruptcy, weeks away from being unable to meet payroll or routine maintenance contracts. A second draft resolution asserts the main building is “unsafe for continued occupancy,” citing a recent water leak that caused the Grand Foyer ceiling to partially collapse.

The resolutions also position Trump’s fundraising skills as the lone hope to keep the institution afloat, with one presenting 10 different options for how the president’s name could be etched onto the building.  

“The Board seeks to provide multiple options so that President Trump can be legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the façade of the Kennedy Center so that he agrees to carry the burden of managing the renovation and provides the Center with a much required financial rescue,” the resolution continues.

The plans were first reported by the Washington Post, which earlier cited confidential documents showing that ticket sales and fundraising have plummeted since the board decided to inscribe Trump’s name in December.

The board of trustees, handpicked and installed by the president, is expected to vote on the two resolutions on Tuesday afternoon. A request for comment was not immediately returned.

That meeting will come just hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper holds a scheduling conference in an ongoing lawsuit brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who has led the legal challenge over the Kennedy Center changes.

“Pay up or the Kennedy Center closes, & the price is Trump’s name on the building,” Norm Eisen, one of the lawyers representing Beatty, wrote Monday on social platform X. “That’s from the board’s meeting materials, one day before they vote on it.”

“An outrageous act of hostage taking,” he added.

Cooper blocked the Kennedy Center from moving forward with a prolonged closure for renovations in late May but allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue. 

He also ordered that Trump’s name be removed from the building’s facade, concluding that the board’s initial decision was unlawful because only Congress had the authority to change the name. 

The lettering was removed in June, but the board voted on a resolution in August that would again re-add his name to the facility in the form of two inscriptions.

Cooper peppered Justice Department lawyers during a hearing last month about why the board was in a rush. The Kennedy Center has agreed to hold off until at least October 8, while also claiming the building may be demolished if the roughly $257 million renovation project is not allowed to move forward.

“The Kennedy Center is in terrible trouble,” DOJ lawyers wrote in previous court filings. “The crisis is so acute that, without the Trump Administration, its people, and President Trump, the Center cannot survive, either structurally or financially.”

data.title: GLP-1-driven vitamin deficiency linked to rare brain disorder: Study
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A new study found that a rare but serious brain condition has been identified in a small number of people taking popular weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Wernicke encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder caused by a severe deficiency of vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

Researchers identified 15 cases reported in 2023 and 2024 among people taking GLP-1 medications containing semaglutide, found in Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, found in Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Vitamin B1 is essential for proper nerve function. Without enough of it, patients can develop confusion, problems with balance and coordination, and abnormal eye movements.

If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent brain damage or death. Physicians consider it a medical emergency.

GLP-1 drugs can contribute to vitamin deficiencies by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake, including foods rich in vitamin B1, such as pork, fish and whole grains.

The study found that most patients who developed the condition also experienced severe vomiting, loss of appetite, poor nutrition or rapid weight loss.

While the disorder remains rare, researchers said the findings should help doctors educate patients about the risk and monitor for warning signs.

data.title: Russian drone almost hit former CIA director; may have targeted Boris Johnson
data.description:
Former CIA Director David Petraeus on Sunday was at a Ukrainian train station while a Russian drone hit a passenger train not long after a diplomatic train carried former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other foreign officials.

The Ukrainian state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, stated that the diplomatic train was at the border between Ukraine and Poland after exiting the station at Yahodyn. Ukraine’s Central Monitoring Group, the dispatch unit that tracks aerial threats, notified the train’s passengers and crew to evacuate.

The alert was transmitted “literally 15 minutes before” the drone hit the train, according to a translated Telegram post.

“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” Ukrainian railway officials said.

Petraeus told The New York Times that he heard the drones fly over his train, leaving Ukraine after he attended a security conference in Kyiv. He heard an explosion shortly after he and other passengers evacuated the train.

“This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians,” he told the Times in a phone interview.

Johnson rode with national security advisers from several European Union and NATO member states. He later wrote on the social platform X that the Ukrzaliznytsia staff and their passengers are “absolutely heroic.”

“I don’t know what warped logic drove [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning,” Johnson wrote. “What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day –– even on civilian railways.”

The railway stated that the diplomatic train might have been the target, noting that the train left the station earlier. The country’s rail system adjusts train schedules in response to the frequent threat of Russian attacks.

Petraeus boarded a different train and safely entered Poland. He praised Ukraine’s people as being “truly unbreakable” against Russian attacks.

Russia has intensified its campaign against Ukraine’s infrastructure, including its railways and power grid, ahead of the harsh winter season. The Russian Defense Ministry said it’s targeting “railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries,” CNN reported, citing state news agency TASS.

These attacks have been in response to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s diesel refineries, including in Siberia and the city of Nizhnekamsk, a hub for several refineries.

President Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt the attacks on these refineries, saying that it was “hurting the world.” Diesel prices have soared to $6.23 as of Monday after an average of $3.71 last year, according to AAA.

Zelensky wrote on X on Monday that Ukraine will halt these strikes if Russia agrees to any deals facilitated by European and American partners.

“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” he said.
